abstract: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) must interpret microbial signals to transcriptionally adapt their identity and function. Which transcription factors (TFs) mediate those adaptations, and whether competing transcriptional pathways signal within the same or in different IEC subpopulations, remains unclear. We find that microbiota colonization shifts nearly all IECs toward an interferon-driven inflammatory program at the expense of genes involved in enterocyte differentiation and metabolism. These opposing gene expression programs are associated with different TF motifs and are inversely correlated within individual cells. We discover that HNF4, a TF central to enterocyte differentiation, acts as a brake on interferon signaling in vitro. In accord, loss of HNF4 in IECs in mice elevates baseline interferon-stimulated gene expression but prevents its full induction during infection with the bacterial pathogen Salmonella. Together our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which opposing intestinal epithelial differentiation and interferon signaling programs interact within the same cell to maintain proper transcriptional control and homeostasis.
